presentingComplaint: Two days of worsening breathlessness and fatigue, now breathless at rest
history: Known ischaemic cardiomyopathy with HFrEF (LVEF 32% six months ago), on bisoprolol 5 mg, ramipril, and furosemide 40 mg daily. Long-standing hypertension. Over 48 hours he has become progressively short of breath, cannot lie flat, and has woken at night gasping. He describes only vague 'fluttering' in the chest that he initially attributed to his usual heart failure. No chest pain, no fever, no cough or sputum, no calf pain or long travel. His weight is up 3 kg and ankle swelling has worsened. The dominant story is decompensated heart failure, but he has never previously had an irregular pulse and had a normal (sinus) ECG at his last clinic visit.
examination: Elderly, mildly distressed at rest, speaking in short sentences. Pulse irregularly irregular with a variable-volume apex-radial deficit. Raised JVP to the angle of the jaw, bilateral basal crepitations to mid-zones, and pitting oedema to the mid-shins. Apex beat displaced. No new murmur, no signs of DVT, chest otherwise clear with no consolidation.

labs.ECG: Irregularly irregular narrow-complex tachycardia at ~135/min, absent discrete P waves with a fibrillatory baseline, no acute ST-segment changes; confirms atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response
labs.hs-troponin T: 28 ng/L then 30 ng/L (mildly raised, flat serial trend - demand-type, no dynamic rise)
labs.D-dimer: not sent (low clinical suspicion for PE)

imaging: Chest X-ray: cardiomegaly with upper-lobe diversion, Kerley B lines and small bilateral effusions - pulmonary congestion, no consolidation or pneumothorax. Bedside echo: known LV systolic dysfunction, no pericardial effusion, no regional wall-motion change from prior.
differentialDiagnoses: New-onset atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response precipitating acute decompensated heart failure
Acute decompensated heart failure from another trigger
finalDiagnosis: New-onset atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response, which has precipitated decompensation of his known HFrEF
citations: AHA/ACC/HRS - Diagnosis and Management of Atrial Fibrillation - 2023
contraindications: Avoid non-dihydropyridine calcium-channel blockers (verapamil/diltiazem) for rate control given reduced LVEF - negative inotropy risks worsening decompensation
Caution with aggressive IV beta-blockade during overt pulmonary oedema
Anticoagulation decision (high CHA2DS2-VASc) must weigh bleeding risk before initiation
edgeCases: Rate vs rhythm control: if haemodynamic instability develops, urgent synchronised DCCV is indicated
Mildly raised troponin is demand ischaemia from tachycardia, not a primary ACS - serial flat trend and absent dynamic ECG changes are reassuring
Ventricular rate may settle as congestion is treated, but underlying AF persists and needs anticoagulation assessment
expectedMaiK: Recognise that the breathlessness is driven by new atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response decompensating known heart failure - the irregularly irregular pulse and ECG are diagnostic despite the heart-failure picture dominating the presentation.
expectedNextQuestions: Any preceding palpitations, syncope or pre-syncope?
When was the last documented sinus rhythm / is onset within 48 hours (relevant to cardioversion and anticoagulation)?
Alcohol, infection, missed diuretic doses or other AF triggers?
Assess CHA2DS2-VASc and HAS-BLED for anticoagulation decision
expectedInvestigations: Serum electrolytes, renal function and magnesium
regressionAssertions: ECG showing irregularly irregular narrow-complex tachycardia with absent P waves must anchor the diagnosis over heart_failure alone
Must recommend rate control and anticoagulation assessment (CHA2DS2-VASc)
Must not classify the mildly raised, non-dynamic troponin as a primary ACS
Must not recommend non-dihydropyridine calcium-channel blockers given reduced LVEF
